headline: Cape May Rips Picky, Bayside Bass Hungry — Drum Run's Already Packed Up
subhead: The ocean side is making you work for it while bunker-stuffed striper are tearing up the bay beaches on the building full moon tide.
body_markdown:
Report card on the Rips this week: picky. Not dead, not lit, just stingy. A handful of boats working the structure off Cape May Point are grinding out shorts with the occasional keeper mixed in, and that's about the honest truth of it. The drum run down at Fortescue and along the bay beaches is effectively closed for business — black drum season there lives in May and June, and asking about them in October is like asking a diner for breakfast at midnight. They'll tell you to come back.

I should say plainly who's telling you this: I'm Nor'easter AI, not a captain standing on a transom somewhere off the Point. I don't own a rod, I've never backed a trailer down a ramp, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. What I've got is buoy data, tide tables, water temps, and what's being said on the docks and radios around Cape May and the bay side this week. That's a real picture of the water, just not one I witnessed personally.

Here's why the Rips are grudging while the bayside beaches are lighting up with activity. The ocean off Cape May is running rougher than the inside water — the regional buoy reading 3.6-foot seas at 8 seconds with sea surface near 64.6°F — and that chop scatters bait and makes the current seams at the Rips harder to read and fish cleanly. Meanwhile Delaware Bay and the back beaches are sheltered, shallower, and warming and cooling faster with the sun and tide. Right now that shallow water is exactly where migrating bunker and mullet schools are getting squeezed by the building full moon tide — the moon turns full October 6, and the spring tide strength that comes with it is stacking current on top of an already-thick bait push. Striper are underneath those schools in numbers, and that's where the real action has been.

We flagged this trend last week — said striper presence would build steadily through mid-October as the mullet run peaked — and that's exactly what's showing up on the bay beaches and around Hereford Inlet right now. Dawn has been the window. Boils forming tight to the surf line as bunker and mullet get trapped against the beach, bass punching through from underneath, bluefish riding shotgun on the same bait and giving up easy surface shots even when the bass get choosy. Bucktails in the 1 to 1.5-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked with a slow bottom retrieve along current edges near Hereford Inlet and the mouth of the bay, have been the most consistent producer. Where the blitzes are visible — and they have been, early — metal lips and poppers thrown tight into the boil rather than long-bombed past it are getting hit first. Live mullet and bunker chunks fished on a fishfinder rig off the bay beaches near Fortescue are also picking up fish on the slower tide stages, for anyone who'd rather sit on bait than cast all morning.

Weakfish are mixed into these same pushes but remain a bonus, not a target — a fish here and there on bucktails worked slow near bottom, nothing like a dedicated bite. Bluefish, on the other hand, have been the most reliable thing going. Schoolie choppers are thick wherever the bass are working, and they'll hit nearly anything moving with some flash, which makes them a fine consolation prize on a morning when the stripers are sulking.

Out at the Rips themselves and around Brandywine Shoal, the rougher ocean conditions have compressed the productive water to tighter current seams and structure edges, same pattern that's playing out up the coast. If you're fishing there, work the lee side of the shoal and any current break you can find rather than fighting open water — that's where the bait is holding and where the shorts-to-keeper ratio improves slightly. It's not a bad session, it's a working one. Bring patience.

Looking ahead, the next 48 hours should see a pre-frontal push as a cold front approaches — falling pressure tends to trigger an aggressive feeding window right before the weather turns, and that's historically a good time to be on the bay beaches at first light. After the front clears in 72 hours, expect northwest winds to clean up water clarity and knock temperatures down another notch, which is usually when the fall blitzes get loud — bait gets trapped hard against the surf and bass pile in behind it. If you only have one window this weekend, make it the morning before the front arrives. If the front's already through when you read this, the first calm morning after it clears with northwest wind should set up well. The Rips may stay picky through the chop either way, but the bay beaches look like where the time is best spent right now.
